text:
Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)
Section 1: Overview
[clause id: CARD-001-S1]

[clause id: CARD-001-S1]

Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES) is a synthetic condition used for this guideline set. Patients typically present with symptoms managed through a stepwise approach involving lifestyle modification followed by pharmacologic therapy with vasodilating agents.

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)

text:
Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)
Section 2: First-Line Management
[clause id: CARD-001-S2]

[clause id: CARD-001-S2]

First-line management of APES consists of initiating Cardaprilol at 5-10 mg once daily, alongside structured lifestyle counseling. Strength of recommendation: Strong.

This applies to patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 45 mL/min/1.73m2 or above. For patients with eGFR between 30 and 44, the starting dose of Cardaprilol should be halved to 2.5-5 mg once daily. Below an eGFR of 30, Cardaprilol should not be initiated at all; a nephrology-cleared alternative should be selected instead (see Section 5).

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)

text:
Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)
Section 3: Second-Line Management
[clause id: CARD-001-S3]

[clause id: CARD-001-S3]

If first-line therapy does not achieve target control within 8-12 weeks, add Rhythmostat at 25-50 mg twice daily. Strength of recommendation: Conditional. Rhythmostat is not recommended as a substitute for Cardaprilol in treatment-naive patients — it is an add-on agent only, not a first-line alternative, even in patients who report difficulty tolerating Cardaprilol's common side effects.

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)

text:
Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)
Section 4: Monitoring
[clause id: CARD-001-S4]

[clause id: CARD-001-S4]

Patients on therapy for APES should be reviewed every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months once stable, with routine labs to screen for treatment-related adverse effects.

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)

text:
Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)
Section 5: Special Populations
[clause id: CARD-001-S5]

[clause id: CARD-001-S5]

For patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 who cannot receive Cardaprilol per Section 2, refer to Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference (SYN-GUIDE-NEPH-003), Section 5, for the specific renal-safe alternative and reduced-dose regimen before initiating any vasodilating agent. Pregnant patients should not receive Rhythmostat under any circumstance, regardless of trimester; Cardaprilol at the lowest effective dose is preferred with obstetric co-management.

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Stage 2 Arterial Pressure Elevation Syndrome (APES)

Cardiology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 1: Overview
[clause id: CARD-003-S1]

[clause id: CARD-003-S1]

This reference summarizes standard dosing and key contraindications for commonly used vasodilating agents in cardiology.

metadata.document_title: Cardiology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Cardiology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 2: Dosing Table
[clause id: CARD-003-S2]

[clause id: CARD-003-S2]

| Drug | Standard Dose Range | Primary Contraindication |
|------|---------------------|---------------------------|
| Cardaprilol | 5-10 mg once daily | severe renal artery narrowing |
| Rhythmostat | 25-50 mg twice daily | second-degree conduction block |
| Flowtensin | 2.5 mg once daily, titrate to 10 mg | pregnancy |

Flowtensin should not be titrated beyond 10 mg once daily under any circumstance; doses above this threshold have shown no additional benefit in the reference population and increase orthostatic hypotension risk.

**Renal dose adjustment (Cardaprilol only):**

| eGFR (mL/min/1.73m2) | Adjusted Dose |
|---|---|
| ≥ 45 | 5-10 mg once daily (standard) |
| 30-44 | 2.5-5 mg once daily |
| < 30 | Do not initiate; select alternative per Section 3 |

metadata.document_title: Cardiology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Cardiology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 3: Contraindications
[clause id: CARD-003-S3]

[clause id: CARD-003-S3]

Each agent listed above should be avoided in the presence of its primary contraindication. Cardaprilol additionally requires caution in patients with a history of hypersensitivity reactions to related compounds.

metadata.document_title: Cardiology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Cardiology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 4: Drug Interactions
[clause id: CARD-003-S4]

[clause id: CARD-003-S4]

Concurrent use of more than one agent from this table requires dose adjustment and increased monitoring frequency, particularly in patients over 65 or with reduced organ clearance.

Care Pathway: Thyroid Hormone Imbalance Disorder (THID)
Section 2: First-Line Management
[clause id: ENDO-002-S2]

[clause id: ENDO-002-S2]

Initial management of THID involves Insulyx at 0.2-0.4 units/kg/day, individually titrated. Strength of recommendation: Strong. This applies to adults under 65 with no cardiac history. Strength of recommendation: Conditional. Insulyx dose increases should not be made in response to a single elevated reading — only after a confirmed pattern across at least two consecutive measurements.

Infectious Disease Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 1: Overview
[clause id: ID-003-S1]

[clause id: ID-003-S1]

This reference summarizes standard dosing and key contraindications for commonly used anti-infective agents in infectious disease.

metadata.document_title: Infectious Disease Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Infectious Disease Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 2: Dosing Table
[clause id: ID-003-S2]

[clause id: ID-003-S2]

| Drug | Standard Dose Range | Primary Contraindication |
|------|---------------------|---------------------------|
| Bactrizole | 500 mg every 8 hours for 7-10 days | known QT prolongation |
| Microfend | 1 g intravenously every 12 hours | severe egg protein allergy |
| Infectiguard-X | 100 mg twice daily for 14 days | concurrent use with anticoagulants |

metadata.document_title: Infectious Disease Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Infectious Disease Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 3: Contraindications
[clause id: ID-003-S3]

[clause id: ID-003-S3]

Each agent listed above should be avoided in the presence of its primary contraindication. Bactrizole additionally requires caution in patients with a history of hypersensitivity reactions to related compounds. Bactrizole should not be combined with Infectiguard-X despite both being oral agents with non-overlapping primary contraindications — the combination is specifically flagged in Section 4 due to additive QT prolongation risk, which is not captured by either drug's individual contraindication alone.

metadata.document_title: Infectious Disease Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Infectious Disease Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 4: Drug Interactions
[clause id: ID-003-S4]

[clause id: ID-003-S4]

Concurrent use of more than one agent from this table requires dose adjustment and increased monitoring frequency, particularly in patients over 65 or with reduced organ clearance. Bactrizole and Infectiguard-X specifically should not be prescribed together: both agents independently carry a mild QT-prolonging effect that is additive in combination, even though neither drug lists the other as a primary contraindication. If both indications are present, complete a full course of one agent before starting the other, with an ECG check prior to switching.

metadata.document_title: Infectious Disease Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Electrolyte Regulation Disorder (ERD)

text:
Care Pathway: Electrolyte Regulation Disorder (ERD)
Section 2: First-Line Management
[clause id: NEPH-002-S2]

[clause id: NEPH-002-S2]

Initial management of ERD involves Filtrexan at 5-10 mg once daily. Strength of recommendation: Strong. This applies when serum potassium is between 5.1 and 6.4 mmol/L. At or above 6.5 mmol/L, this is an urgent presentation per the referral criteria document and initial management should not proceed outpatient — Filtrexan initiation in that range should only begin after acute management in an urgent care setting.

Section 3: Second-Line Management
[clause id: NEPH-002-S3]

[clause id: NEPH-002-S3]

Patients with inadequate response after an appropriate trial period should be reassessed for combination therapy or specialist referral per the referral criteria document for Nephrology. Strength of recommendation: Conditional.

[clause id: NEPH-002-S4]

[clause id: NEPH-002-S4]

Section 1: Overview
[clause id: NEPH-003-S1]

[clause id: NEPH-003-S1]

This reference summarizes standard dosing and key contraindications for commonly used renal-protective agents in nephrology.

metadata.document_title: Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 2: Dosing Table
[clause id: NEPH-003-S2]

[clause id: NEPH-003-S2]

| Drug | Standard Dose Range | Primary Contraindication |
|------|---------------------|---------------------------|
| Nephrostat | 2.5 mg once daily, adjust for eGFR | bilateral renal artery stenosis |
| Kalibind | 15 g once daily with food | bowel obstruction |
| Filtrexan | 5-10 mg once daily | eGFR below 15 mL/min/1.73m2 untreated |

metadata.document_title: Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 3: Contraindications
[clause id: NEPH-003-S3]

[clause id: NEPH-003-S3]

Each agent listed above should be avoided in the presence of its primary contraindication. Nephrostat additionally requires caution in patients with a history of hypersensitivity reactions to related compounds.

metadata.document_title: Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 4: Drug Interactions
[clause id: NEPH-003-S4]

[clause id: NEPH-003-S4]

Concurrent use of more than one agent from this table requires dose adjustment and increased monitoring frequency, particularly in patients over 65 or with reduced organ clearance.

metadata.document_title: Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference

text:
Nephrology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 5: Cross-Specialty Alternative for Severe Renal Impairment
[clause id: NEPH-003-S5]

[clause id: NEPH-003-S5]

For patients who cannot receive Cardaprilol (see Cardiology Care Pathway, SYN-GUIDE-CARD-001) due to an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, Nephrostat may be used as a renal-safe alternative at a reduced dose of 1.25 mg once daily, provided there is no bilateral renal artery stenosis. This reduced dose applies down to an eGFR of 15 mL/min/1.73m2; below that threshold, nephrology co-management is required before initiating any agent from this table.

Care Pathway: Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS)
Section 1: Overview
[clause id: RESP-001-S1]

[clause id: RESP-001-S1]

Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS) is a synthetic condition used for this guideline set. Patients typically present with symptoms managed through a stepwise approach involving lifestyle modification followed by pharmacologic therapy with bronchodilating agents.

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS)

text:
Care Pathway: Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS)
Section 2: First-Line Management
[clause id: RESP-001-S2]

[clause id: RESP-001-S2]

First-line management of CARS consists of initiating Bronchaline at 2 puffs (90 mcg) every 6 hours as needed, alongside structured lifestyle counseling. Strength of recommendation: Strong. Current smokers should be offered a structured cessation program alongside first-line therapy rather than after it — delaying cessation support until second-line escalation is not supported by this pathway.

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS)

text:
Care Pathway: Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS)
Section 3: Second-Line Management
[clause id: RESP-001-S3]

[clause id: RESP-001-S3]

If first-line therapy does not achieve target control within 8-12 weeks, add Airoflux at 250 mcg twice daily via inhaler. Strength of recommendation: Conditional. Airoflux is not an as-needed rescue inhaler and should not be prescribed in place of Bronchaline for acute symptom relief — it is a scheduled maintenance add-on only.

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS)

text:
Care Pathway: Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS)
Section 4: Monitoring
[clause id: RESP-001-S4]

[clause id: RESP-001-S4]

Patients on therapy for CARS should be reviewed every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months once stable, with routine labs to screen for treatment-related adverse effects.

metadata.document_title: Care Pathway: Chronic Airway Restriction Syndrome (CARS)

Respiratory Medicine Comorbidity Management Pathway
Section 2: Common Comorbidities
[clause id: RESP-005-S2]

[clause id: RESP-005-S2]

The most frequently observed comorbidities in this population are osteoporosis from long-term steroid exposure and deconditioning. Screening for these should occur at routine follow-up visits, except in the following cases where screening frequency should increase to every visit rather than annually:
- Cumulative oral steroid courses exceeding 4 per year
- Prior fragility fracture at any site
- Age 70 or older regardless of steroid exposure

[clause id: RHEU-001-S2]

Care Pathway: Chronic Joint Inflammation Syndrome (CJIS)

[clause id: RHEU-001-S3]

text:
Care Pathway: Chronic Joint Inflammation Syndrome (CJIS)
Section 4: Monitoring
[clause id: RHEU-001-S4]

[clause id: RHEU-001-S4]

Patients on therapy for CJIS should be reviewed every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months once stable, with routine labs to screen for treatment-related adverse effects. Additional monitoring applies when on immune-modulating therapy:
- Screen for latent infection before starting any immune-modulating agent, not only in patients with known risk factors
- Do not resume therapy after an active infection until it has fully resolved, even if disease activity is worsening in the interim

text:
Rheumatology Agent Dosing and Contraindication Reference
Section 2: Dosing Table
[clause id: RHEU-003-S2]

[clause id: RHEU-003-S2]

| Drug | Standard Dose Range | Primary Contraindication |
|------|---------------------|---------------------------|
| Immunoflex | 10-25 mg once weekly (see hepatic adjustment below) | active untreated tuberculosis |
| Jointral | 200 mg twice daily | pre-existing retinal disease |
| Autostem | 5 mg twice daily | active severe infection |

**Hepatic dose adjustment (Immunoflex only):** patients with mildly elevated liver enzymes (up to 2x upper limit of normal) may continue at the standard dose with monthly monitoring. Above 2x upper limit of normal, the dose should not simply be reduced — therapy should be held entirely until enzymes normalize, then restarted at the lowest dose (10 mg).
